issues.legal_issue: A revisional court cannot interfere with a decision in a landlord-tenant possession suit on a question of statutory interpretation when the court deciding the suit had jurisdiction to entertain it.
material_facts: The landlord brought a suit to recover possession from a tenant, and the trial court had jurisdiction to hear landlord-tenant possession suits.
The tenant challenged the eviction decision on the interpretation of the statutory grounds for recovery of possession.
The appellate court decided the appeal, and the tenant sought revision of that decision.
issues.conclusion: The revision application was incompetent because the lower courts had jurisdiction to decide the suit and the interpretation question; the High Court could not interfere in revision even if the appellate court had erred on the facts or law.
issues.legal_principle: Section 28 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, vested the specified court with jurisdiction over landlord-tenant suits concerning possession and excluded other courts, subject to an exception not applicable here. Because the trial court had jurisdiction over the suit, it also had jurisdiction to interpret the grounds for eviction; an error in exercising that jurisdiction would not make the decision open to revision.

predicates.landlord_tenant_possession_suit: A landlord brought a proceeding against a tenant seeking possession of premises.
predicates.lower_court_had_jurisdiction: The court deciding the proceeding had authority to hear landlord-tenant disputes seeking possession.
predicates.revision_challenge_concerns_an_issue_wit: The party seeking revision challenged the lower court's determination of an issue arising within its authority to decide the possession proceeding.

issues.definition: When a landlord-tenant possession suit is decided by a court with authority to hear it, a revision challenge to an issue within that authority does not permit revisional interference.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord's bona fide and reasonable requirement of premises for the landlord's own occupation is not displaced by a plan to alter or rebuild the premises before occupying them.
material_facts: The landlord sought possession of the entire house for personal residential use, including the portion occupied by the tenant.
The landlord said the old house was unsafe and that he would use it for his own residence after necessary alterations and repairs.
The courts below found that the landlord bona fide required the premises for his occupation.
The tenant argued that the planned work meant the claim fell under the statutory ground for demolition and construction rather than the ground for the landlord's own occupation.
issues.conclusion: The landlord's claim fell under the own-occupation ground despite the intended alterations. That ground applies where the landlord reasonably and bona fide requires the premises for the landlord's own occupation, whether or not alterations are needed first. The demolition-and-new-building ground applies where the landlord does not require the premises for own occupation but seeks to erect a new building to let to tenants.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 13(1)(g) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, a landlord may recover possession when the premises are reasonably and bona fide required for the landlord's own occupation. Section 13(1)(hh), read with sections 13(3A) and 17A–17C, addresses demolition to erect a new building for letting to tenants; those provisions impose construction undertakings and provide protections and rights for displaced tenants. Section 17 protects against misuse of the own-occupation ground if the premises are not occupied or are re-let. The Court relied on Krishnalal Ishwarlal Desai v. Bai Vijkor, [1964] 1 SCR 553, concerning occupation under the Act; Krishna Das v. Bidhan Chandra, AIR 1959 Cal 181; McKenna v. Porter Motors Ltd., [1956] AC 688; and Betty's Cafes Ltd. v. Phillips Furnishing Stores Ltd., [1959] AC 20. It declined to follow the contrary approach in Manchharam Ghelabhai Pittalwala v. Surat Electricity Co. Ltd. and Allarkha Fakirmahomed v. Surat Electricity Co. Ltd.

predicates.rent_control_possession_case: A landlord seeks possession from a tenant in a proceeding governed by rent-control protections.
predicates.landlord_reasonably_and_bona_fide_requir: The landlord has a reasonable and genuine need to use the premises for the landlord's own occupation.
predicates.landlord_plans_alterations_before_occupa: The landlord intends to alter, repair, or rebuild the premises before occupying them.

issues.definition: If a landlord in a rent-controlled possession case genuinely and reasonably needs the premises for own occupation and plans work before occupying them, the own-occupation ground applies notwithstanding that work.
